title: Euenius · lines 33–40
subtitle: Herodotus describes the sacred flock of Apollonia and the men who guard it; this year it is Euenius' turn

units.en: In Apollonia there are sheep sacred to the Sun. By day they graze beside a river; by night they are guarded by men chosen from the citizens most distinguished for wealth and birth, each man serving for a year.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The verb comes first, as in a description of a place, so the reader knows Herodotus has stepped aside from his main story to tell a tale.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: The sheep are called sacred before we are even told they are sheep, so the reader knows from the start that harming them will be serious.

notes.label: Contrast (μέν ... δέ)
notes.quote: τὰς μὲν ἡμέρας … τὰς δὲ νύκτας
notes.body: The balanced phrases divide the flock's day in two, which shows a careful routine that runs round the clock.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: A calm picture of sheep grazing by a river, which makes the slaughter to come all the more shocking.

notes.label: Pairing
notes.body: Linking the two with τε καί shows that the guards must be both rich and well born, so guarding the flock is an honour.

notes.label: Superlative
notes.body: Only the very best citizens are chosen, which shows how much the flock matters to the city.

notes.label: Present tense
notes.trans: graze … guard … set store by … spend the night
notes.body: The custom is described in the present, as if it still goes on, so the reader feels Apollonia is a real place they could visit.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: The idiom, strengthened by δή, stresses how highly the Apollonians value the flock, so the reader expects them to react strongly to any loss.

notes.label: Foreshadowing
notes.body: The flock is tied to the gods from the start, which hints that the gods will step in later in the story.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.trans: a long way from the town
notes.body: Far away comes at the end of the sentence, so the reader notices how isolated the cave is, a place where something could go wrong unseen.

notes.label: Polyptoton
notes.body: The same verb appears for the guards and for Euenius, which reminds the reader that he is one of the chosen elite.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: Two adverbs and δή pin down one place and one moment, so the reader knows the description is over and the story is starting.

notes.label: Change of tense
notes.body: After a run of present tenses the imperfect marks the move from custom to event, so the reader feels the story begin.

notes.label: Apollonia
notes.body: A colony of Corinth and Corcyra on the Adriatic, in modern Albania. In his fuller account Herodotus says the river the sheep graze beside flows down from Mount Lakmon to the sea near the harbour of Oricum.

notes.label: The Apollonians
notes.body: The people of Apollonia. The ending -ιᾶται is a common way of forming the name of a city's citizens.

notes.label: Euenius
notes.body: Known only from this story. Herodotus tells it because Euenius' son Deiphonus served as seer to the Greek fleet at Mycale in 479 BC.

questions: Why might Herodotus describe the custom of guarding the flock in such detail before telling us anything about Euenius?
What does the choice of guards tell you about how the Apollonians regard the sheep?

context.body: The tale of Euenius comes in Book 9 of the Histories, in the middle of the campaign of 479 BC. Before the battle of Mycale, fought on the coast of Asia Minor opposite Samos, the sacrifices for the Greek fleet were made by a seer called Deiphonus, and Herodotus stops to explain who Deiphonus' father was and how the family came by its gift of prophecy. The story has nothing to do with the war. It is there because Herodotus thinks it worth telling, and because it says something about how gods deal with men.

Apollonia was a Greek city near the Adriatic coast, in what is now Albania, founded around 600 BC by colonists from Corinth and Corcyra. Many Greek sanctuaries kept animals that belonged to a god: they could not be sold, eaten or used like ordinary livestock, and harming them was an offence against the god himself. This flock belongs to Helios, the Sun, who had less of a cult of his own than the Olympian gods; but Greek audiences knew another sacred flock of the Sun from Book 12 of the Odyssey, where Odysseus' starving crew kill and eat the Sun's cattle and are all destroyed for it.
